Cantankerous describes a person who is bad-tempered, grumpy, and genuinely difficult to get along with — someone who argues, complains, and causes trouble regularly, often over small or unimportant things.

The key thing to understand is that cantankerous is not about a one-time bad mood. It describes a personality trait — a habitual, persistent way of being. A cantankerous person is almost always like this. They are quick to find fault, quick to disagree, and hard to please. Crucially, cantankerous also carries a strong sense of stubbornness. A cantankerous person doesn't just get upset — they dig their heels in. They resist reason, refuse to cooperate, and can be nearly impossible to negotiate with. This combination of bad temper plus stubbornness plus persistence is what makes the word uniquely powerful and more specific than simpler words like "grumpy" or "irritable."
What it looks like in real life

Picture a neighbour who complains your music is too loud even when it clearly isn't. When you try to calmly explain, they argue. When you offer a solution, they refuse it. When you give up and walk away, they call after you with another complaint. That is cantankerous behaviour — the grumbling, the arguing, the refusal to cooperate, all rolled into one difficult person.
Who or what can be described this way

It most commonly describes people, and is especially (though not exclusively) used for older individuals who have grown set in their ways and short on patience. It can also describe animals — a cantankerous old mule, for example, is one that bites, kicks, and refuses to cooperate no matter what you do. In informal, humorous contexts, people even apply it to objects: "that cantankerous old engine" for a car that constantly breaks down and resists being fixed.

This is a vivid, expressive word. It is slightly informal but not slang — you will find it in novels, newspapers, and everyday conversation. Interestingly, it often carries a faintly humorous or even affectionate quality. Calling someone cantankerous is more colourful and almost playful compared to calling them simply "difficult" or "unpleasant." Writers often use it to describe grumpy-but-harmless characters in a way that makes the reader smile rather than recoil.
How it differs from similar words

Grumpy means being in a bad mood, but it's milder and more temporary. Irritable means being easily annoyed, but again, it's more in-the-moment. Quarrelsome focuses specifically on picking fights. Crotchety is very close to cantankerous and is often used for old people in particular. Ornery is also very similar, but more common in American English and more informal. Cantankerous is the richest of the group because it bundles bad temper, stubbornness, and a persistent pattern of behaviour all into one word.
A person who is the opposite of cantankerous would be described as easy-going, good-natured, amiable, agreeable, or pleasant.

"The cantankerous old man refused to return the ball that rolled into his yard, and argued loudly with anyone brave enough to knock on his door."

"She grew cantankerous as the meeting dragged past midnight — snapping at colleagues and rejecting every compromise on the table."

"Despite his cantankerous reputation, the professor secretly left encouraging notes on struggling students' papers."

That last sentence captures something important: the word is often used when there is a gruff, difficult exterior that might be hiding something more complex underneath. Cantankerous characters in literature are frequently the ones who turn out to have a hidden warmth — the grumpiness is their armour, not their soul.
